Guide

Moving off paper registers without losing a term

For the principal and the office About 7 minutes

The failure mode is not the software. It is starting in the wrong month, typing up too much history, and switching everything on the same day. Any of the three can cost a school a term of confidence, after which the staff quietly go back to the register and the software becomes a thing nobody opens.

Start at the right point in the year

The best month to start is the first month of a new session, because that is the one month where the opening balances are simple: almost nobody is carrying arrears and the roll has just been settled.

The second best is any month, starting with fees only, taking the arrears each family owes as an opening figure and not typing up the history behind it. The worst is the middle of admission season, when the office has no spare attention, or the week before exams.

What to type up, and what to leave alone

This is where most of the wasted effort goes. The instinct is to bring everything across. Do not.

RecordBring acrossWhy
Current pupils Yes, all of them Nothing works without the roll. This is the one unavoidable job.
Fee structure per class Yes Small, and every challan depends on it being right.
What each family owes today Yes, as one opening figure One number per family, not a history. This is the whole trick.
Old receipts and past months No Weeks of typing to reproduce a book you still own and can still open.
Past attendance No Nobody will ever query last March from the new system.
Past exam marks Only the current session, if a result card is due Otherwise it is data entry with no reader.
Staff records Yes, current staff Needed for logins and for staff attendance.

Keep the paper. Nothing above says throw it away. It stays in the cupboard and it stays readable, and once a year somebody will be glad of it.

What a clean import actually needs

Almost every school has its pupils in Excel already. Whether that file imports in one pass or needs three days of correction comes down to a handful of things:

  • One row per pupil. Not one row per family with three children in adjacent columns, which is the most common shape we see and the most expensive to unpick.
  • A single column for the class, spelled the same way every time. "Class 5", "5", "V" and "Five" in one column is four classes as far as any importer is concerned.
  • The father's name and one phone number, in their own columns. The phone number is what links siblings into a family and what a reminder is eventually sent to.
  • Dates in one format. Pick one and make the whole column match. A column containing both 03/09/2026 and 9-Mar-26 cannot be read safely, because the first is ambiguous on its own.
  • No merged cells, no colour as meaning. A row highlighted yellow to mean "left the school" carries information no file format preserves. Put it in a column.

An importer that accepts a broken file silently is worse than one that refuses it. If a row cannot be read, the right behaviour is to reject the whole file, say which row and why, and let you fix the sheet: half an import is the hardest state to recover from.

Run both for two weeks

This is the step schools want to skip and the one that decides the outcome. For two weeks, the clerk writes the paper receipt and enters it. Yes, it is double work. It buys three things:

  1. Proof. At the end of a fortnight you have two independent totals for the same period. If they agree, the school believes the software. If they do not, you find out now rather than in March.
  2. Practice under real conditions. A clerk learns the screen with a parent standing in front of them, which is the only way anybody learns a counter system.
  3. A way back. If something is genuinely wrong, you stop, and you have lost two weeks of extra typing rather than a term of records.

After two weeks of agreement, stop writing the paper receipt for fees. Keep the attendance register for another month if the teachers want it. Let them drop it when they trust it, and they will, because the phone is faster than the book.

The order, in one list

  1. Classes and sections.
  2. Fee heads and the amount for each class.
  3. Pupils, imported from your spreadsheet.
  4. Opening arrears, one figure per family.
  5. Staff, and logins for the teachers who will mark attendance.
  6. One class of attendance, for one week, with one teacher.
  7. The whole school's attendance.
  8. Fees, in parallel with paper, for two weeks.
  9. Fees, on their own.
  10. Exams, at the next assessment.
  11. The parent portal, once the balances are known to be right.

The portal is last on purpose. The moment parents can see a balance, that balance has to be correct, because a wrong figure in front of four hundred families is a different kind of problem from a wrong figure in an office.

How this works in The School Manager

The importer refuses a file it cannot read completely, and names the row and the reason, so a half-finished import is not a state you can reach. Opening arrears are a supported starting figure rather than something you have to fake with a fabricated challan. The parent portal is off until you turn it on. And there are sixteen chapters walking through exactly this order in the handbook, free to read before you buy anything.
